title: How Oral Traditions Survive Without Any Text
text:
Long before writing was widespread, societies stored history, law and poetry in memory alone and passed them on by voice. The obvious question is how anything of that length survives transmission when there is no text to check it against.

The classic answer came out of fieldwork. In the nineteen-thirties Milman Parry and Albert Lord travelled through the Balkans recording singers who performed epic poems lasting hours. What they found was not memorisation. The singers composed as they performed, assembling each line from a stock of ready-made phrases that fitted the rhythm, and building scenes from standard episodes such as the arming of a hero or the arrival of a messenger. Ask a singer to repeat a song and the wording changed, while the story held. Parry and Lord then reread the Homeric epics in this light and argued that their repeated phrases were the fingerprint of the same oral technique. The wider lesson for anthropology is that an oral tradition is not a degraded version of a written archive. It has its own devices for accuracy: rhythm, formula, repetition, and an audience that knows the material well enough to object. What such a tradition preserves reliably is structure and meaning rather than exact wording.
points: The question is how long oral works survive accurately with no written text to check them against.

The singers composed while performing, using ready-made phrases that fitted the rhythm and standard scenes.
Repeat performances changed in wording while the story stayed the same.
They argued the repeated phrases in the Homeric epics show the same oral technique.
Oral tradition has its own accuracy devices and preserves structure and meaning rather than exact wording.
